newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Separatist leader visits Georgia for first time.
newsitem.headline: Separatist leader visits Georgia for first time.

text.p: The leader of Georgia's breakaway Abkhazia region arrived in the capital Tbilisi on Thursday for unprecedented face-to-face peace talks with President Eduard Shevardnadze.
Reuters reporters saw Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba arriving together with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, who has been mediating the talks.
They were immediately driven to a Shevardnadze residence and went immediately into talks with the Georgian leader.
Ardzinba's visit is the first to Georgia since he became leader of Abkhazia and comes five years to the day since Georgian troops entered the province to put down a move towards independence.

"Russia is doing everything to end this conflict which has taken the lives of so many people," Primakov told reporters before talks started. "Those who think that Russia is not doing enough are mistaken. Let's hope everything will be successful."
Talks between Georgia and Abkhazia on reaching a full political agreement have been deadlocked and the latest round of U.N.-mediated negotiations has produced no tangible results.
The subtropical Black Sea region has run itself as a de facto independent state since the brutal 1992-93 ethnic conflict between the two sides in which some 10,000 people were killed.
Heavy security was in place around the city airport in advance of the arrival of Primakov and Ardzinba. Primakov's visit had been previously announced.
Primakov has said he hopes to prepare a deal between Georgia and Abkhazia to pave the way for a formal peace agreement to be signed in Moscow in the presence of President Boris Yeltsin.

Yeltsin has lately supported the Georgian position that Abkhazia should be part of Georgia but receive wide autonomy, and that the separatist government should allow at least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees to return to their homes.
Abkhazia wants confederation. This has been repeatedly rejected by Tbilisi.
Russia also has 1,500 peacekeepers in a buffer zone between Abkhazia and Georgia.

The mandate for the Russian force expired on July 31 but they will apparently stay in the zone until their fate can be decided by the leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) which groups 12 former Soviet republics in September.

Georgia wants the peacekeepers to police more of Abkhazia and help resettle refugees. Commonwealth leaders approved the changes earlier this year but Russia has refused to take them up, citing Abkhaz objections.
Shevardnadze has urged Moscow not to ease sanctions against Abkhazia imposed two years ago by the CIS leaders.

A partial sea blockade, enforced almost entirely by Russian naval vessels, and strict restrictions on movement through the region's only land border with Russia have crippled Abkhazia's once thriving tourist-driven economy.
